nameStory: This deep-sea flatfish gets its name from the frigid waters around Greenland where it thrives in the icy depths. The name 'halibut' comes from 'holy butt' - medieval folks called it the 'holy flatfish' because it was often eaten on religious holidays. Interestingly, a fjord in Greenland is actually named Hellefisk Fjord after this very fish, using the Danish word 'hellefisk' for Greenland halibut.
description: The Greenland halibut is a deep-sea flatfish that's quite different from its bottom-dwelling cousins. Unlike most flatfish that lie flat on the seafloor, this species can actually swim upright in the water column like a regular fish. Both sides of its body are colored (rather than having one pale side), with speckled brown coloration that's darker on the right side and paler on the left. It's a large predatory fish that inhabits the cold, deep waters of the northern oceans.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Distinctive flatfish shape but swims vertically rather than lying flat - imagine a flounder standing up and swimming like a regular fish through the water column

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Both sides are speckled brown with darker mottling, but the right side is noticeably darker than the left side - unusual for a flatfish which typically has one pale side

idTips.label: Eyes
idTips.description: Both eyes are on the right side of the head, but the left eye hasn't migrated as far as in other flatfish, allowing the fish to see forward while swimming upright

idTips.label: Habitat
idTips.description: Found in extremely deep, cold water between 500-1,000 meters deep - you'd only encounter this fish through deep-sea fishing or research vessels

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: A substantial fish reaching impressive sizes typical of halibut species, with a robust, muscular body built for life as an active predator in deep waters

habitat: In New England waters, Greenland halibut inhabit the deepest, coldest parts of the continental shelf and slope, typically at depths of 500-1,000 meters where temperatures remain near freezing year-round. These fish prefer the frigid waters far offshore where the ocean floor drops into the deep Atlantic. You'd only encounter this species through deep-sea commercial fishing operations or research vessels, as they're far beyond the reach of recreational fishing.

seasonality.spring: Deep-water fish maintain consistent behavior year-round due to stable deep-sea conditions. Any seasonal movements are related to following prey rather than temperature changes.
seasonality.summer: Continues hunting in the deep, cold waters regardless of surface temperature changes. May follow schools of deep-water fish that make up their diet.
seasonality.fall: Remains in deep waters where temperature and light conditions stay constant throughout the year, unaffected by surface seasonal changes.
seasonality.winter: Active in the deep where conditions mirror the frigid surface temperatures, potentially moving into slightly shallower waters during the coldest months.

funFact: This flatfish caused an actual international conflict called the 'Turbot War' in the 1990s between Canada and Spain over fishing rights - though thankfully it was a bloodless 'war' fought with coast guard vessels and harsh diplomatic words rather than weapons!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with other halibut species, but the Greenland halibut's ability to swim upright and its darker coloration on both sides distinguishes it from bottom-dwelling flatfish. Remember: if you see a flatfish swimming vertically with both sides colored, you're looking at a Greenland halibut.
contextualKnowledge: In North America, this fish is often called 'turbot' (Greenland turbot or Newfoundland turbot), but this can be confusing since true turbot is a completely different European fish. The various common names - black halibut, blue halibut, lesser halibut - reflect regional fishing traditions and the fish's variable appearance in different conditions.
compareHints: As the only member of its genus Reinhardtius, the Greenland halibut is unique among North Atlantic flatfish for its upright swimming behavior and bilateral coloration. Compared to other righteye flounders in its family, it's distinguished by its incomplete eye migration, vertical swimming posture, and preference for much deeper, colder waters than typical bottom-dwelling flatfish. Most other flounders in New England waters are smaller, live in shallower water, and lie flat on the bottom.
